item.title: Apple Announces September 14 Release Date for iOS 27 and Other Updates
item.description:
Apple Announces September 14 Release Date for iOS 27 and Other Updates

Apple has announced that its next generation of software updates, first unveiled at WWDC26, will be released on Monday, September 14. These updates will be available as free downloads for compatible devices across the Apple ecosystem.

⚙️ Key details

The updates introduce major upgrades including design refinements, performance improvements, and updates to various apps. A primary focus of the release is the introduction of new Apple Intelligence and Siri AI features.

Operating System Key Features and Improvements
iOS 27 Siri AI, Apple Intelligence, Visual Intelligence, expanded customization, and upgrades to Photos, Safari, Messages, Mail, Passwords, Shortcuts, and Home
iPadOS 27 Apple Intelligence features and iPad-specific productivity improvements
macOS 27 Golden Gate Siri AI, Visual Intelligence, Apple Intelligence features, and performance improvements
watchOS 27 New Siri, fitness, health, and Smart Stack capabilities

🚀 Availability

In addition to the major operating systems, Apple is releasing tvOS 27, visionOS 27, HomePod software 27, and new AirPods firmware on September 14. Following developer betas in June and public betas in July, users can install the updates via the following methods:

  • iPhone and iPad: Settings > General > Software Update
  • Mac: System Settings > General > Software Update
  • Apple Watch: Through the Watch app on a paired iPhone
  • Apple TV and Apple Vision Pro: Through Settings

#Apple #iOS27 #AppleIntelligence #SiriAI #SoftwareUpdate

Source: Apple confirms release dates for iOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27 and more

item.title: Apple Introduces Siri Audio Intelligence Features with On‑Device Privacy Protections
item.description:
Apple Introduces Siri Audio Intelligence Features with On‑Device Privacy Protections

Apple announced a handful of new Siri AI Audio Intelligence features — Siri Recap, Live Rewind, Sound Recognition, and Music Recognition — at the iPhone Duo launch event, accompanied by a privacy‑focused technical document.

🔍 Overview

  • Siri Recap – summarizes recent interactions.
  • Live Rewind – lets users double‑tap the Digital Crown to replay recent audio.
  • Sound Recognition – identifies ambient sounds.
  • Music Recognition – detects music playing nearby.

🧩 How it works

  • Audio is captured by the microphone and immediately routed into the Secure Enclave of the S11 chip found in Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4.
  • The Secure Enclave is a hardware‑isolated compartment that processes sensor data separately from the rest of the system.
  • Within the Enclave, audio is analyzed for speech, sounds, or music without transcribing or storing the raw audio.
  • Processed data lives in a continuously overwritten buffer that never creates an audio recording and is not saved as a file.
  • If results need to move to an iPhone, they are encrypted and transferred through the Secure Enclaves of both devices.

⚙️ Key details

  • The raw audio is not accessible to the operating system, apps, or Apple.
  • Users control when Audio Intelligence features are active; for example, Live Rewind requires a double‑tap of the Digital Crown each time.
  • Users decide what text to keep from Siri Recap and Live Rewind.
  • Kept text syncs with end‑to‑end encryption when a device passcode and iCloud two‑factor authentication are enabled.
  • Apple states it cannot access users’ raw audio from these features.

#Apple #Siri #AudioIntelligence #Privacy

Source: Read the Apple document explaining how new listening features still protect your privacy

item.title: Apple Unveils iPhone Duo Foldable and iPhone 18 Pro Lineup
item.description:
Apple Unveils iPhone Duo Foldable and iPhone 18 Pro Lineup

At the “Surprise and Shine” event in Cupertino on September 9, Apple officially unveiled a new generation of hardware, including its first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo, alongside the iPhone 18 Pro series, Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4, and AirPods 5. AI serves as the common thread across this new ecosystem.

📱 iPhone Duo

The iPhone Duo is Apple’s first foldable iPhone, featuring a Grade 5 titanium build and a precision-engineered hinge with more than 100 components.

  • Displays: A 7.6-inch Super Retina XDR inner display (more than 50% larger than the iPhone 18 Pro Max) and a 5.4-inch external display.
  • Durability: IP68 rating and Ceramic Shield 2 on the outer display, which Apple claims has up to three times greater scratch resistance than the previous generation.
  • Performance: Powered by the A20 Pro chip, utilizing a dual-battery architecture and a vapor-chamber cooling system.
  • Display Tech: Supports ProMotion and Always-On capabilities with a peak outdoor brightness of 3,000 nits.
  • Expanded Utility: Support for Apple Pencil USB-C is coming later this year for sketching, note-taking, and document annotation.

📸 iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max

These models focus on AI, battery life, performance, and camera capabilities, powered by the A20 Pro chip and a new-generation vapor-chamber cooling system for high sustained performance.

  • Camera System: Features a 48MP Fusion main camera with variable aperture. The system can automatically optimize aperture for depth of field and lighting, or users can manually select from four levels.
  • Video and Audio: Supports 4K Dolby Vision HDR time-lapse and cinematic effects applied after recording at up to 60 fps. Audio Mix has been improved for voice processing.
  • Imaging: Additional Photographic Styles controls for image grain and texture.

⌚ Apple Watch Series 12

Powered by the S11 chip, the Series 12 introduces a Health Sensing System combining electrical and optical sensors to measure heart rate variability (HRV) and heart rate every five seconds.

  • AI Integration: watchOS 27 brings Siri AI to the device to combine personal context with broader knowledge. New Audio Intelligence capabilities will arrive later this year.
  • Materials: Available in aluminum, titanium, and a ceramic option (available in Night and Pearl White).

⚙️ Key Details

Product Colors Storage / Materials Price / Availability
iPhone Duo Star White, Night Sky 256GB to 2TB Starts at $1,999; Sales Oct 23
iPhone 18 Pro / Pro Max Black, Silver, Glacier, Burgundy N/A Retail availability Sept 18

🚀 Availability

  • iPhone Duo: Pre-orders begin October 16; sales start October 23. Available in more than 70 countries, including Vietnam.
  • iPhone 18 Pro / Pro Max: Pre-orders begin September 12; retail availability starts September 18. Vietnam is included in first-wave pre-orders.

#Apple #iPhoneDuo #iPhone18Pro #AppleWatch #AI

Source: Apple Unveils New Product Lineup: Foldable iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro, Apple Watch Series 12 and AirPods 5 - TechTimes.vn

item.title: Apple to hold Surprise and shine presentation on September 9, 2026
item.description:
Apple to hold Surprise and shine presentation on September 9, 2026

Apple has announced its annual autumn presentation, titled “Surprise and shine,” scheduled for September 9, 2026. This event marks the first major presentation under the leadership of new CEO John Turnus. The broadcast will begin at 10:00 Pacific Time and will be available via the Apple website, Apple TV, and YouTube.

🔍 Overview

The event is expected to prioritize premium devices, with a focus on high-end hardware. Anticipated announcements include:

  • The first foldable iPhone
  • iPhone 18 Pro
  • iPhone 18 Pro Max

⚙️ Key details

The foldable iPhone is expected to feature a clamshell design, offering a standard external display that unfolds into a compact tablet. Reports indicate the external OLED display will measure approximately 5.5 inches.

Device Feature Expected Detail
Foldable iPhone Design Clamshell, tablet-sized internal screen
iPhone 18 Pro/Max Camera Possible variable aperture
Software Siri New generation powered by Apple Intelligence

Additional expectations for the new iPhone lineup include updated processors, improved battery life, camera upgrades, and further reduction of the elements surrounding the Dynamic Island.

🚀 Availability

Following the focus on premium devices at this autumn event, more affordable models are expected to be carried over to a spring 2027 launch. Analysts suggest the foldable iPhone may be priced between $2,000 and $2,500 depending on the configuration. Long-term projections suggest this category could generate tens of billions of dollars in revenue by the end of 2027.

#Apple #iPhone #Technology #AppleIntelligence #Foldable

Source: Apple Event 2026: what Apple will unveil on 9 September

item.title: Apple Seeks Expedited Discovery in Legal Dispute with OpenAI
item.description:
Apple Seeks Expedited Discovery in Legal Dispute with OpenAI

Apple is requesting “expedited discovery” in its ongoing legal battle against OpenAI, citing concerns regarding the destruction of forensic evidence. The dispute centers on three former Apple employees who transitioned to OpenAI, including Chang Liu.

⚙️ Key details

  • Apple alleges that OpenAI failed to inspect a company-owned MacBook used by Liu, despite having it in their possession since July.
  • OpenAI provided the laptop to Apple on August 21st. An inspection of the device allegedly revealed that Liu downloaded a confidential Apple circuit schematic and used it in his work at OpenAI.
  • Apple claims messages on the device show Liu discussing the need to “restore” and “start using” Apple-owned equipment after learning of an internal investigation in June.
  • Apple maintains there is a “real risk of evidence destruction” regarding transient data such as logs, metadata, and usage records.
  • OpenAI argues that the dispute stems from Apple’s own “mess” of an employee exit process.
  • OpenAI states there is no evidence that Liu accessed Apple information for improper purposes, noting he has “no use for Apple confidential information.”

#Apple #OpenAI #Lawsuit #Legal

Source: Apple accuses OpenAI of destroying evidence

item.title: Phil Schiller Steps Back from App Store and Apple Events Role
item.description:
Phil Schiller Steps Back from App Store and Apple Events Role

Apple Fellow Phil Schiller is officially reducing his operational responsibilities, stepping down from overseeing the App Store and Apple product launches as the company prepares for a leadership transition to incoming CEO John Ternus.

🔍 Overview

  • Schiller is stepping down from overseeing the App Store and Apple product launches
  • He will retain only his Apple Fellow role
  • The move coincides with John Ternus set to take over as Apple CEO
  • The App Store is returning to Eddy Cue, who oversaw it until 2015

⏰ Background and Workload

  • In 2024, The Wall Street Journal reported Schiller was working close to 80 hours a week
  • As Apple Fellow, Schiller continued to oversee the App Store and Apple events, but the role may not have left him with sufficient time for his own endeavors
  • Schiller was present with Steve Jobs and Tim Cook at the start of Apple’s comeback in 1997–1998
  • He has a combined 35 years of service to Apple: 1987–1993 and 1997 to today

🔄 Organizational Changes

Role Person Details
App Store oversight Eddy Cue Previously oversaw it until 2015; will take more influential role under Ternus
Day-to-day App Store operations Carson Oliver Longtime App Store team member
Apple CEO (incoming) John Ternus Will lead as Schiller steps back
  • Cue is Apple’s services chief and will reportedly be taking a more influential role under Ternus’ leadership
  • Carson Oliver, who has long been on the App Store team, will oversee its day-to-day operations

📋 What This Means

  • Schiller is officially stepping back to only his Apple Fellow role
  • The App Store returns to Eddy Cue after nearly a decade under Schiller
  • Leadership restructuring appears timed to coincide with the CEO transition to Ternus

#Apple #PhilSchiller #AppStore #leadership #JohnTernus #EddyCue

Source: Michael Tsai

item.title: SOTA OCR On-Device with Core ML and dots.ocr
item.description:
🔧 SOTA OCR On-Device with Core ML and dots.ocr

Converting cutting-edge OCR models for seamless on-device deployment

Power efficiency comparison across different compute units

Every year our hardware is a little more powerful, our models a little smarter for each parameter. In 2025, it is more feasible than ever to run truly competitive models on-device. dots.ocr, a 3B parameter OCR model from RedNote, surpasses Gemini 2.5 Pro in OmniDocBench, making OCR a truly no compromises on-device use case. Running models on-device is certainly appealing to developers: no smuggling API keys, zero cost, and no network required. However, if we want these models to run on-device, we need to be mindful of the limited compute and power budgets.

Enter the Neural Engine, Apple’s custom AI accelerator that has shipped with every Apple device since 2017. This accelerator is designed for high performance whilst sipping battery power. Some of our testing has found the Neural Engine to be 12x more power efficient than CPU, and 4x more power efficient than GPU.

Apple’s Neural Engine architecture visualization

Whilst this all sounds very appealing, unfortunately the Neural Engine is only accessible through Core ML, Apple’s closed source ML framework. Furthermore, even just converting a model from PyTorch to Core ML can present some challenges, and without a preconverted model or some knowledge of the sharp edges it can be arduous for developers. Luckily, Apple also offers MLX, a more modern and flexible ML framework that targets the GPU (not the Neural Engine), and can be used in conjunction with Core ML.

In this three part series, we will provide a reasoning trace of how we converted dots.ocr to run on-device, using a combination of CoreML and MLX. This process should be applicable to many other models, and we hope that this will help highlight the ideas and tools needed for developers looking to run their own models on-device.

🚀 Getting Started

To follow along, clone the repo. You’ll need uv and hf installed to run the setup command:

1

./bootstrap.sh

If you just want to skip ahead and use the converted model, you can download it here.

🔄 Conversion

Converting from PyTorch to CoreML is a two step process:

  1. Capturing your PyTorch execution graph (via torch.jit.trace or, the more modern approach of torch.export).
  2. Compiling this converted graph to an .mlpackage using coremltools.

Whilst we do have a few knobs we can tweak for step 2, most of our control is in step 1, the graph we feed to coremltools.

Following the programmers litany of make it work, make it right, make it fast, we will first focus on getting the conversion working on GPU, in FLOAT32, and with static shapes. Once we have this working, we can dial down the precision and try and move to the Neural Engine.

🧩 Dots.OCR

Dots.OCR consists of two key components: A 1.2B parameter vision encoder trained from scratch, based on the NaViT architecture, and a Qwen2.5-1.5B backbone. We will be using CoreML to run the vision encoder, and MLX to run the LM backbone.

📊 Step 0: Understand and simplify the model

In order to convert a model, it’s best to understand the structure and function before getting started. Looking at the original vision modelling file, we can see that the vision encoder is similar to the QwenVL family. Like many vision encoders, the vision encoder for dots works on a patch basis, in this case 14x14 patches. The dots vision encoder is capable of processing videos and batches of images. This gives us an opportunity to simplify by only processing a single image at a time. This approach is frequent in on-device apps, where we convert a model that provides the essential functions and iterate if we want to process multiple images.

When kicking off the conversion process, it’s best to start with a minimal viable model. This means removing any bells and whistles that are not strictly necessary for the model to function. In our case, dots has many different attention implementations available for both the vision encoder and the LM backbone. CoreML has lots of infrastructure oriented around the scaled_dot_product_attention operator, which they introduced in iOS 18. We can simplify the model by removing all of the other attention implementations and just focusing on simple sdpa (not the memory efficient variant) for now.

Once we’ve done this, we see a scary warning message when we load the model:

1

Sliding Window Attention is enabled but not implemented for `sdpa`; unexpected results may be encountered.

The model doesn’t require Sliding Window Attention to function, so we can happily move on.

⚡ Step 1: A simple harness

Using torch.jit.trace is still the most mature method for converting models to CoreML. We usually encapsulate this in a simple harness that allows you to modify the compute units used and the precision selected.

You can check out the initial harness. If we run the following on the original code implementation:

1

uv run convert.py --precision FLOAT32 --compute_units CPU_AND_GPU

We should bump into the first (of many) issues.

🐛 Step 2: Bug hunting

It is rare that a model will convert first time. Often, you will need to progressively make changes further and further down the execution graph until you reach the final node.

Issue 1: Data Type Mismatch

Our first issue is the following error:

1
2

ERROR - converting 'outer' op (located at: 'vision_tower/rotary_pos_emb/192'): In op "matmul",
when x and y are both non-const, their dtype need to match, but got x as int32 and y as fp32

Luckily this error gives us quite a bit of information. We can look at the VisionRotaryEmbedding layer and see the following code:

1
2
3

def forward(self, seqlen: int) -> torch.Tensor:
 seq = torch.arange(seqlen, device=self.inv_freq.device, dtype=self.inv_freq.dtype)
 freqs = torch.outer(seq, self.inv_freq) return freqs

Although torch.arange has a dtype argument, coremltools ignores this for arange and always outputs int32. We can simply add a cast after the arange to fix this issue.

Issue 2: Repeat Interleave

After fixing this, running the conversion again leads us to our next issue at repeat_interleave:

1

ERROR - converting 'repeat_interleave' op (located at: 'vision_tower/204'): Cannot add const [None]

Whilst this error is less informative, we only have a single call to repeat_interleave in our vision encoder:

1
2

cu_seqlens = torch.repeat_interleave(grid_thw[:, 1] * grid_thw[:, 2], grid_thw[:, 0]).cumsum(
 dim=0, dtype=grid_thw.dtype if torch.jit.is_tracing() else torch.int32, )

cu_seqlens is used for masking variable length sequences in flash_attention_2. It’s derived from the grid_thw tensor, which represents time, height and width. Since we are only processing a single image, we can simply remove this call.

Issue 3: Dynamic Index

Onto the next! This time, we get a more cryptic error:

1
2

ERROR - converting '_internal_op_tensor_inplace_fill_' op (located at:
'vision_tower/0/attn/301_internal_tensor_assign_1'): _internal_op_tensor_inplace_fill does not support dynamic index

This is again due to the masking logic to handle variable length sequences. Since we are only processing a single image (not a video or batch of images), we don’t really need attention masking at all! Therefore, we can just use a mask of all True. To prepare ourselves for the Neural Engine conversion, we also switch from using a boolean mask to a float mask of all zeros, as the Neural Engine does not support bool tensors.

Issue 4: Reshape Compatibility

With all of this done, the model should now successfully convert to CoreML! However, when we run the model, we get the following error:

1

error: 'mps.reshape' op the result shape is not compatible with the input shape

This reshape could be in multiple places! Luckily, we can use a previous warning message to help us track down the issue:

1
2
3
4

TracerWarning: Iterating over a tensor might cause the trace to be incorrect. Passing a tensor
of different shape won't change the number of iterations executed (and might lead to errors or
silently give incorrect results).
 for t, h, w in grid_thw:

Most ML compilers do not like dynamic control flow. Luckily for us, as we are only processing a single image, we can simply remove the loop and process the single h, w pair.

And there we have it! If we run the conversion again, we should see that the model successfully converts and matches the original PyTorch precision:

1

Max difference: 0.006000518798828125, Mean difference: 1.100682402466191e-05

📈 Step 3: Benchmarking

Now that we’ve got the model working, let’s evaluate the size and performance. The good news is the model is working, the bad news is that it’s over 5GB! This is completely untenable for on device deployment! To benchmark the computation time, we can use the built in XCode tooling by calling:

1

open DotsOCR_FLOAT32.mlpackage

which will launch the XCode inspector for the model. After clicking + Performance Report and launching a report on all compute devices, you should see something like the following:

Performance report showing over a second for a single forward pass

Over a second for a single forward pass of the vision encoder! We have lots of more work.

In the second part of this series, we will work on the integration between CoreML and MLX, to run the full model on-device. In the third part, we will dive deep into the optimizations required to get this model running on the Neural Engine, including quantization and dynamic shapes.

🙌 Credits

Originally posted at: https://huggingface.co/blog/dots-ocr-ne

🏁 Conclusion

Converting state-of-the-art models like dots.ocr for on-device deployment presents unique challenges but offers significant benefits in terms of privacy, cost, and offline functionality. This first part of our series demonstrated the iterative process of identifying and resolving conversion issues when moving from PyTorch to Core ML.

Key takeaways include:

  • Start Simple: Begin with minimal viable models and gradually add complexity
  • Expect Issues: Model conversion rarely works on the first attempt
  • Understand Your Model: Deep knowledge of the model architecture helps in debugging
  • Optimize Progressively: Follow the “make it work, make it right, make it fast” principle

While we’ve achieved a working conversion, the 5GB model size and slow inference times highlight the optimization work still ahead. The Neural Engine’s power efficiency advantages make this effort worthwhile for production on-device applications.

#COREML #OCR #ONDEVICE #NEURALENGINE #PYTORCH #MLX #APPLE #AI #OPTIMIZATION
